From Strategy to complete System
Let us say you are a highly motivated new trader and 
-You read few good books.
-Watched some great YouTube videos.
-Followed successful traders on X.
-Eventually, you found a setup that makes sense.
Maybe it's pullback,VCP, or EP
At this point, almost 98% think they've found "the edge" and stops .
They've only completed Layer 2 in the image
Your setup is just one component of a complete trading process.

This how you create whole System
Layer 1 -Choose Your Game
Before you study charts, decide what game you're playing.
-Intraday
-Swing
-Position
-Investing
Every timeframe demands different rules, expectations, position sizing & psychology.

Layer 2- Find 1/2 Repeatable Setup
Examples:
-Pullbacks
-VCP
-Momentum Bursts
- etc.
This is very easiest step as 99% on X are talking only about this

Layer 3 -Build the Process (The Real Work)
This is where a setup becomes a trading system.
-Which stocks qualify(scan)?
-What is my exact entry trigger(Entry)?
-Where is my stop-loss(SL)?
-How much do I risk(Risk)?
-How do I size positions(Position Size)?
-How do I manage open trades(Portfolio Risk)?
-When do I exit(Tarde Management)?
They should already exist as written rules.

Layer 4 - Understand Market Context
The exact same setup can produce completely different outcomes depending on market conditions.
Ask first:
-Is the market trending?
-Is this a normal pullback?
-Is the market range-bound?
Great traders know when their edge exists and when it doesn't.

Layer 5 - Execute Like a Professional
Once the system exists, psychology becomes much simpler.
Your job is to simply fearless execution.

That requires:
-Discipline
-Thinking in probabilities
-Judging results over a series of trades not one trade

The Ultimate Skill
Once you understand these five layers, you can read a Market Wizards interview, watch a presentation by Minervini, Qullamaggie, David Ryan or any successful trader and immediately reverse-engineer their complete trading process.

That's the difference between collecting strategies and becoming a system builder.
Bookmark this and refer every time you are creating a system

Most traders think risk management means knowing where their stop is.

That matters, but it’s only trade-level risk.

The bigger question is: what happens to the entire portfolio if several things go wrong at once?

That is portfolio-level risk management, and it changes the way I think about exposure completely. 🧵

Another important concept is open risk.

If every current position went against me and every stop was hit, how much would the portfolio lose?

That number should always be known.

But even open risk needs context, because not every position in the portfolio is carrying the same type of risk.

A fresh position that was entered this morning is very different from a position that has already moved in my favor, been partially trimmed, and had its stop raised.

They may have the same market value, but they no longer represent the same portfolio risk.

That distinction becomes extremely important when deciding whether I can add more exposure.

You can have 10 individually well-sized trades and still be carrying far too much risk.

If most of those positions are semiconductors, high-beta growth, small caps, momentum names, or crypto-related equities, you may think you own 10 separate trades when, in reality, you’ve expressed the same underlying bet several times.

That is why I don’t look at position size in isolation. I also care about concentration, correlation, and how many positions are likely to respond to the same market move.

Different tickers can still be the same trade.

The question is not only, “How much can I lose on this position?”

It is also, “What happens if this entire pocket of the market gets hit?”

This is also why I use NER — Net Exposure Risk.

For me, one of the most useful things NER does is help sequence exposure progressively, especially by focusing on the part of the portfolio still made up of new, unproven positions that haven't been de-risked yet.

When I first enter a trade, I am still carrying the initial risk. The stock has not proved itself, I have not taken anything off, and I have not reduced the stop distance.

If I add too many positions in that stage at once, I may create a portfolio that looks reasonable by gross exposure but is actually carrying a large amount of fresh risk.

That is exactly what I want to avoid.

So I don’t think of exposure as something I deploy all at once.

I want to sequence it.

As existing positions start working, I can trim into strength, raise stops, or otherwise reduce the amount of capital at risk. That creates room for new positions.

Exposure is earned progressively as trades prove themselves.

A portfolio with 80% exposure made up mostly of de-risked winners is very different from a portfolio with the same 80% exposure made up entirely of fresh entries.

This also means you can't decide position sizing without looking at the rest of the book.

Your first position and your tenth position are not necessarily the same decision, even if both setups look equally attractive.

By the time you are considering that tenth trade, you may already have several positions carrying fresh risk, several correlated exposures, and a lot more portfolio heat than when you opened the first one.

That is why I ask a different question before adding a trade:

“What does this position do to the portfolio?”

Does it add a new source of exposure, or just more of something I already own?

Am I adding it while previous positions have already been de-risked, or am I stacking another fresh trade on top of several others that have not proven themselves yet?

That context can completely change how aggressively I size the trade — or whether I take it at all.

The goal is not to maximize exposure.

It is to maximize the quality of exposure.

I want the portfolio to expand as the market proves itself and as individual positions prove themselves. When breadth is healthy, trends are persistent, and my existing trades are working, risk can increase progressively.

When conditions deteriorate, volatility expands, stops begin getting hit, or fresh trades stop following through, I want the opposite process to happen.

Exposure comes down.

That is what I mean when I say risk should breathe with the market.

Good portfolio risk management is not about avoiding losses. Losses are part of trading.

It is about making sure that no cluster of fresh positions, no single theme, and no sudden change in market conditions can do disproportionate damage to the account.

Because your edge can only compound if you stay in the game long enough to keep applying it.

$QQQ is starting to seriously outperform $QQQE again, meaning the cap-weighted Nasdaq is pulling away from its equal-weight counterpart.

That usually tells you leadership is becoming more concentrated in the biggest names.

What makes it interesting now is the starting point: the $QQQ / $QQQE relationship just bounced from a deeply oversold -2σ extreme.

So this isn’t just mega-caps leading.

It’s mega-cap leadership coming back from a major washout.

If this continues, the generals are back in charge.

Semis may be starting to regain their footing vs software.

The $SMH / $IGV relationship has cooled off a lot from its earlier highs, but after a meaningful reset it’s trying to stabilize and turn back up.

That matters, because this ratio is really a read on where leadership is concentrating inside tech.

When semis lead, it usually tells you the market is leaning into the more cyclical, higher-beta, infrastructure side of tech. When software leads, the tone is often different.

Right now, this relationship looks less like exhaustion and more like a reset after a big run.

If semis start taking back relative strength here, that would be an important change in character inside tech leadership.

This is a great question, and I think the progression of why I monetize part of my content is worth explaining.

I am an optimist who believes in the good of others, probably to a naive degree.

Back in 2022, after leaving Trillium, I started spending more and more of my time mentoring traders, both online and in person. My hope was that if I helped people become successful, many of them would give back to charity or pay it forward to other traders.

What I learned instead is that most traders don’t give back. Most view PNL and money as their scorecard, and once they earn it, they don’t want to part with it. There is often an “I earned this on my own” mentality.

My naive hopes were pretty badly wrong, and I got burned multiple times. There have absolutely been some very generous exceptions—shoutout to DL @ KTG, NH, AA, and others—but they were exceptions.

So I eventually found myself in a strange position: I was giving away my time and knowledge, helping already-successful traders make even more money, and then hoping afterward that some of that value would make its way toward causes I cared about. Usually, it didn’t.

The same thing happens with free content more broadly. When something is offered for free, people tend to value it accordingly.

A good example is the annual TraderLion conference. It gets 500k+ views, helps thousands upon thousands of traders, and is built around raising money for charity. Yet despite all of that reach and all of the value being provided, it barely raises a few thousand dollars each year.

That experience changed how I thought about this.

I realized I needed to let capitalism do its job. If people receive something they believe has real financial value, they should pay for it. That is why I initially started a Patreon where 100% of the money went to charity.

The course was the more formal extension of that idea. I spent roughly a year building the service I wish I had when I was developing as a trader.

So yes, if you want me to review your trades, answer your specific questions, teach you the details of my edge, or give you access to the highest-value parts of what I’ve learned over my career, you need to pay for it. 

Charging allows me to put a price on something that has value to the person receiving it, and then I can direct that money toward causes I believe in rather than hoping people voluntarily do it afterward (shocker - they don’t).

That is ultimately why I monetize part of my trading education. I started as a naive optimist who assumed that if I gave enough value away, people who benefited would give back. Experience taught me that incentives work much better than hope.

TL;DR: I do charity work and run a nonprofit, but helping traders make more money is not the nonprofit. @Impact_Comp is. If someone receives meaningful value from my trading knowledge, I believe they should pay for it, and monetization gives me the ability to direct that value toward causes I care about.
